extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers (especially short story writers), literary students, and readers interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: An interview-based set of craft observations and standards about writing short stories (and related forms), how influence works, and practical/esthetic expectations for writers. Emphasizes habits, influence phases, form choice, and qualities of strong short fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: The work itself over persona
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s almost as if these young writers... were in a way writing in order to be Hemingway, rather than writing to be a writer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing to cultivate a public persona or celebrity; the idealization of writer-celebrities can eclipse the actual work. Focus on producing work rather than performing an identity—the publicity around famous writers often obscures the daily labor of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write consistently and accept years of obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order to be a writer I have to actually write. And be obscure for many, many years, and be grateful if I get contributors’ copies from some little magazine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes persistence and daily practice (e.g., Hemingway’s disciplined desk work, Frost as a workhorse). The career often involves long stretches with little public recognition—treat writing as work rather than immediate fame-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short story qualities: incisiveness, velocity, exactitude, precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Wolff: he’s “always been attracted to the incisiveness, velocity, exactitude, precision of the short story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concentrated energy and formal precision in short fiction—tightness of language, momentum, and exactitude of detail are virtues of the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form chooses the writer; match form to your imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: “Forms have a way of choosing us... something about our natural appetites... will lead us toward one particular form or another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that your temperament and subject-size will incline you toward certain forms (short story vs. expansive novel). Work within the form that suits your imagination rather than forcing a mismatched large scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate to learn, but don’t try to write like someone else
rubrics_metrics.description: “You have to start somewhere, as an imitator—it’s how we learn... then... I want to write this well. Not write like him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imitation as a learning method to grasp technique and perspective, but convert that learning into a personal standard of excellence rather than stylistic copying. Aim to write stories as good as those you admire, not to replicate their voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness is deceptive and requires lapidary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking of Hemingway: “The plainness is totally deceptive, and is the result of lapidary work, and a way of looking at things that is completely beyond you when you begin.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake simple, plain prose for easy prose. Achieving clarity and plainness often requires meticulous revision and disciplined attention to what is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence evolves in phases: reader → stylistic emulation → aspirational standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Wolff: there are “maybe three phases of influence... books that make you a reader; meeting a style that becomes a way of looking at things; finally... a kind of influence that sets the standard by which you want your own work to be read.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand influence as developmental: early reading creates appetite; mid-phase emulation teaches craft; mature influence sets qualitative goals. Use each phase productively and expect the nature of influence to change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance objectivity with genuine feeling (avoid chilliness or sentimentality)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Katherine Anne Porter and Chekhov: Porter’s work has “a purity, an emotional texture… that nevertheless is not sentimental,” and Chekhov’s “objectivity… was nevertheless infused with emotion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for an emotional clarity that feels truthful without tipping into sentimentality or a detached coldness. Emotional effect should arise from precise, controlled observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The writer tells personal concerns through imagined others
rubrics_metrics.description: “What writers do is they tell their own story constantly through other people’s stories. They imagine other people, and those other people are carrying the burden of their struggles, their questions about themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters and narrative situations to dramatize the writer’s recurring thematic concerns (identity, estrangement, authenticity) rather than confessional exposition; shape the narrator’s perspective to reveal the authorial preoccupations indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of critical detachment that distances you from reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding the critic in “Bullet in the Brain”: his critical faculty “has so overwhelmed him that he’s completely detached from reality at the end.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a demeaningly sneering or overly derisive stance toward material; excessive criticality can blunt empathy and impede authentic engagement with characters and scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisiting early work: know when a ‘vanished’ earlier self is different
rubrics_metrics.description: Wolff on early stories: “I don’t know that I could actually write that story now... None of us are the same after 30 years... I’m not good at seeing what the difference is.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When revising or assembling collections, be mindful that earlier work may reflect a different writerly self. Consider whether revision preserves what was valuable or erases an authentic historic voice; readers may perceive changes more readily than the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary publishing realities: do it for love; be realistic about venues and pay
rubrics_metrics.description: “The venues for short fiction are so diminished... We who write short stories pretty much depend on literary journals now to publish our work, and they don’t have much money... do it because we have to, because something compels us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that opportunities and remuneration for short fiction are limited; pursue publication strategically but recognize that passion for the form, not money, is often the primary motivator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to make readers feel what affected you (aspirational standard of influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wolff on mature influence: reading a great story inspires “I want to write a story that affects others the way this story just affected me.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the emotional impact of works you admire as a concrete goal: strive to produce comparable effects on readers through craft, clarity, and emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural choices: containment of time, cast, and viewpoint can make novels feel story-like
rubrics_metrics.description: On novels he prefers: imagining a novel “as having a limited time-frame and a limited cast and limited circumstances, with a single point of view... structurally, the containment of time, dramatis personae—a story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your imagination leans to concentrated focus, design longer works with contained scope—limited cast, time-frame, and POV—to preserve the short story’s precision within a longer form.
